content.title: About
content.content: Garlic (Allium sativum) is a bulbous flowering plant closely related to the onion, shallot, and leek. Native to Central Asia and northeastern Iran, it has been a staple culinary seasoning and traditional herbal medicine worldwide for thousands of years, known for its pungent flavor and health properties.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crushing or chopping garlic activates alliinase, producing its active organosulfur compound, allicin.
Ancient Greek Olympic athletes consumed garlic to enhance performance.
Black garlic is produced by aging whole bulbs under controlled heat and humidity.
China produces over 70% of the global garlic supply.
Garlic bulbs can be stored for months under appropriate ventilation.

items.title: Cardiovascular Support
items.content: Helps maintain blood pressure levels within normal ranges and supports arterial health.

items.title: Immune Defense
items.content: Organosulfur compounds demonstrate broad antimicrobial and immune-supporting activity.

items.title: Antioxidant Properties
items.content: Contains antioxidants that protect cellular structures from oxidative damage.

items.title: Lipid Regulation
items.content: May assist in maintaining healthy total and LDL cholesterol balance.

items.title: Digestive Irritation
items.content: Raw garlic can cause heartburn, reflux, or stomach irritation in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Bleeding Risk
items.content: May inhibit platelet aggregation; stop high medicinal doses prior to surgery.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mince or crush garlic and let it sit for 10 minutes before cooking to maximize allicin formation. Excellent in roasts, sauces, marinades, and dressings.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole unpeeled bulbs in a cool, dry, dark place with good air circulation. Do not refrigerate whole garlic as it encourages sprouting.
